rv.q: You’d be hard-pressed to see anything else quite this alive and energised in the theatre.
Full of energy and passion, every wonderfully radiant minute in Jaja’s salon is something to savour.
When the play finishes – as if mid-sentence, just as word of a drama involving ICE agents reaches the salon – it feels all too soon.
It is gloriously performed, with heart and masses of character, and directed exuberantly by the talented Touko.

Still, until then the good vibes hold your attention in Jaja’s African Hair Braiding, a play, first staged at the Manhattan Theatre Club in 2023, which offers an exuberant glimpse of West African immigrants building new lives.
For all its flaws though, Jaja’s African Hair Braiding vividly sketches in unseen lives.
Workplace plays don’t come more buoyant and bursting with heart than Jaja’s African Hair Braiding.
The emotional beats pack as much of a punch as the brilliant cast's comedic timing, making each character feel larger than life and that little piece of Harlem feel utterly real.
It would be hard to not fall for the charm of Jaja’s African Hair Braiding.
Nonetheless, Bioh has a talent for creating authentic and culturally specific stories that resonate with all audiences.

Under Monique Touko, who also directed the Lyric's excellent School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, the cast hit just the right energy levels, vibrant without being anarchic, effortlessly funny but leaving space for the sadness in their lives.
Jaja's African Hair Braiding sparkles and shines where it needs to, offering big laughs and moments of poignancy.

cn.t: Bioh's vibrant, Tony-nominated comedy set in a Harlem hair salon wins critics over with its infectious warmth, abundant charm, and buoyant energy, celebrating a sisterhood of West African braiders through humor and heart.
